body:
As far as I can tell from the docs it is not possible to configure Temporal to make use of Postgres read-only replicas to off-load `select` calls from the primary server.

I don't think it needs further explanation as to why this is a good idea. 😉

comments.body:
this sounds interesting @udf2457 
do you have any proposals or design for it ??
is there anything in temporal will be affected using read-replicas??

Thanks @raman20 

I'm not intimately familiar with the temporal code and there is quite a lot of abstraction going on in relation to database code which makes it a little tricky to have a "quick look"

But if my attempt at a "quick look" is correct, all calls (`select` or otherwise) seem to ultimately  rely on the database abstracted in this struct  ? https://github.com/temporalio/temporal/blob/c9ec833cb0180a5f8da21736c59869ac87cbdeb0/common/persistence/sql/sqlplugin/postgresql/db.go#L27

In which case at a high-level you have two main design options:

1. Extend the struct with a specified replica instance (and obviously push down the config parameters accordingly); or
2. Handle multiple replicas - in which case you would clearly need something a little more elaborate because you would need to introduce round-robin of replicas with timeouts.

Clearly with both options you would need a timeout/error driven fallback mechanism to selecting on the primary with both options.  But I would think this should be fairly straightforward ?

I am not sure I follow your second question _"is there anything in temporal will be affected using read-replicas??"_

Do you mean adversely affected ?  No, by definition not.  If anything `select` queries should be more responsive  in busier environments because they are reading off the replica(s), which in turn doesn't get held up by the write activity on the primary.

Officially the read-replicas in Postgres are "eventually consistent", but in practice unless you're doing WAN replication or some-such then most people should find Postgres replication almost instant.   Certainly there are lots of people out there doing high-volume `selects` off replicas, Let's Encrypt is perhaps the most famous where they have one master and multiple replicas and they issue millions of SSL certificates off that.  They use MySQL and that is also "eventually consistent" on replicas.  So I don't think "eventually consistent" should be seen as a deal-breaker, its more of a docs caveat thing (i.e. "monitor it in your environment" and "be careful with WAN replication" etc.).

The postgres docs go in to more detail on this subject, in the Hot Standby section: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/hot-standby.html

There may be a way of doing synchronous replication in Postgres as outlined in this presentation but I've never used it myself: https://www.postgresql.eu/events/pgconfde2025/sessions/session/6559/slides/663/Myths%20and%20Truths%20about%20Synchronous%20Replication%20in%20PostgreSQL.pdf

I don't think you can use the assumption that replication lag is almost instant in the code base. If code in temporal depends on information being instantly available after a write it would be an issue. The application code would need to take that into account, i.e. retry if the information is not yet available.

@jontro Fair point, but I suspect it is largely theoretical since my guess is that Temporal as a whole is "eventually consistent" anyway.  As far as I am aware from a brief RTFM, Temporal makes no promises in relation to synchronicity ?

Hello @udf2457, Temporal logic assumes database is strongly consistent for almost all the write operations. Violating read after write consistency can easily cause a request to return an unexpected non-retryable errors, or even worse leading to execution getting stuck and never make progress.

We are also not accepting any different persistence layer implementation at this point due to team capacity and maintenance overhead. To use a different persistence implementation, you can inject it using the `WithCustomDataStoreFactory` server option defined in `temporal/server_option.go`. We are considering exposing an even lower injection point for sql plugin but there's no concrete timeline on that yet.

Hi @yycptt I hear what you're saying, but I still think you're missing the point. The key question being "Does **_everything_** need to hit the postgres primary ?".

For example, the low-hanging fruit would be the Temporal Web UI.  That is a human point-and-click experience, mostly or entirely based around `SELECT` calls and so would be an ideal use-case for calling against postgres secondary server(s), no ?

title: Enable use of of database replicas
